seo.title: Karmic tail 21 19 7 compatibility: the World, the Sun, the Chariot
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 19 7 compatibility: the World at the entry, the Sun in the middle, the Chariot as the main task, and an Indian myth of the Sun's wife.

title: The 21-19-7 karmic tail in compatibility: the Sun's wife and a team of two
short: Book Ten of the Rigveda describes a wedding to which "all the world" comes, and a bride who vanishes from it. The groom is Vivasvat, the Shining One. Later texts call him the Sun outright and tell the rest of the story: the bride could not bear his light, left a shadow in her place and fled as a mare, and her husband found her only when he became a horse himself. The World, the Sun, the Chariot: the cards of the couple's karmic tail 21-19-7 stand in the same order. The couple enters its shared task wanting a whole world for two and lives that task brightly, in full view, and in that light one partner can start to shine while the other quietly slips into the shadow. The main task is the Chariot: learning to run in one harness so that nobody has to disappear.

sections.h2: How the 21-19-7 tail is built and why only a couple can have it
paragraphs: A couple's tail belongs to neither partner. Each of its points is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Here is an example with the dates 02.01.1980 and 14.04.1975.

The first partner has day 2, month 1 and year 1 + 9 + 8 + 0 = 18. Their karmic task is 2 + 1 + 18 = 21, their centre 42 → 6, their personal tail 9-3-21. The second partner has day 14, month 4 and year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. The karmic task is 40 → 4, the centre 44 → 8, the personal tail 12-16-4. Now the points of the two tails are added in pairs:
This couple's centre is 6 + 8 = 14, Temperance, and the couple's values are 6, The Lovers. Both cards will be needed later.

A personal matrix cannot hold this triple. There the middle of the tail is the reduced sum of the entry and the main task: 21 + 7 = 28 → 10, The Wheel of Fortune. A couple's middle is not recalculated from its two ends; it is added up from the middles of two people, and instead of the Wheel it comes out as the Sun, a number that only two people can produce. The method does not reduce numbers up to 22, yet the Wheel can still be read in the digits of the Sun: 1 + 9 = 10. It is worth remembering: in the myth it will turn up as the lathe on which the Sun is cut down.

The 21-19-7 tail falls to roughly one couple in 269 (0.371%), which puts it 66th among the 97 couple tails. In 98% of these couples it is made of the personal tails 12-16-4 and 9-3-21, as in the example; in 2% it is made of 18-6-15 and 3-13-10. In the main variant the couple's World is built from The Hanged Man and The Hermit, two cards in which a person is alone: one has stopped in a pause, the other has walked away from people. The Sun is built from The Tower and The Empress, a sudden blow and abundance. The Chariot comes from The Emperor and The World, power and a whole world. These are not the partners' roles, because a personal tail is read differently. This is what the numbers are made of, and it says a great deal: this couple's wish for a whole world grows out of two solitudes.
This tail has no permutations. The entry of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 7 and 19 cannot stand there, and no pair of birth dates produces the order 21-7-19.

sections.h2: A myth older than the cards: the Shining One and the Swift One
paragraphs: The oldest version takes up two stanzas of the Rigveda (X, 17, 1–2). In Ralph Griffith's translation (1896):

"Tvaṣṭar prepares the bridal of his Daughter: all the world hears the tidings and assembles. But Yama's Mother, Spouse of great Vivasvān, vanished as she was carried to her dwelling. From mortal men they hid the Immortal Lady, made one like her and gave her to Vivasvān. Saraṇyu brought to him the Aśvin brothers, and then deserted both twinned pairs of children."

The hymn says nothing more: not why she vanished, not where she went. The whole story is told by the Puranas, written down many centuries later: the Markandeya Purana (cantos 77–78) and the Vishnu Purana (book III, chapter 2). The daughter of the heavenly craftsman marries the Sun and cannot bear his radiance. She makes a body of her own out of shadow, leaves it in her husband's house in her place and goes to her father. Her father sends her back to her husband, and she goes north instead, to the Northern Kurus, and lives there as a mare. The Sun lives with the shadow for a long time and never notices the substitution, until the deceit comes out through the children. Then the Sun himself asks his father-in-law to reduce his radiance, takes the form of a horse and finds his wife. From that meeting the Ashvins are born, the twin horsemen of the sky.

The names in this story speak for themselves. Vivasvat means "the Shining One". Saranyu means "the Swift One", from a root meaning "to run, to flow". In the Puranas the bride is called Sañjñā, and among the meanings of the word the Monier-Williams dictionary gives "agreement, mutual understanding, harmony". The double is called Chhāyā, "Shadow". In the Puranas the bride's father is Vishvakarman, "the Maker of All". The cards of the tail sit in these names almost word for word. The World is the wedding to which all the world comes, and the father who made everything. The Sun is the groom. The Chariot is the bride whose name is Swift. And the bride's second name, Agreement, is exactly what the couple has at the entry to its task: a common language.

The story reaches beyond India. A nineteenth-century Sanskrit dictionary notes that some scholars connected the name Saranyu with the Greek Erinys. And Pausanias recorded an Arcadian myth in which Demeter turned into a mare to escape Poseidon, he caught her in the form of a stallion, and for her anger at this the goddess was called Erinys there (Description of Greece, VIII, 25).

sections.h2: The World at the entry: a wedding the whole world comes to
paragraphs: For Yuliana Lisovskaya, the entry to the task is the point of shared wishes and agreements, the couple's "common language". It sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also become resistance. This couple has the World at the entry, and its wish is the size of the world.

Couples like this begin with something big. They have not yet decided where to live, but they already know which countries they will travel to, what the house will be like, whom they will invite to the table and how they will look at life. They agree quickly, and they are at ease together on the road, in a move, in a strange city. From outside they often look like the perfect couple. Waite calls the World "the perfection and end of the Cosmos", and at the entry this is exactly what the couple wants: a whole in which nothing is missing.

The Rigveda adds one detail to this picture, and it is unsettling. The whole world gathered for the wedding, and the bride vanished on the way, in the wedding procession itself, "as she was carried to her dwelling". Nobody noticed, because she was replaced by "one like her". The Sanskrit word, savarṇā, literally means "of the same colour". This is where the World's minus in a couple begins: the picture stays whole, but the person is no longer in it.

In everyday life this looks ordinary. The couple still has shared plans, shared friends, shared photographs. But one partner has long been the only one talking about "our world", while the other nods. Decisions get made, but there is no agreement: nobody has checked it since it put itself together in the first months. Lisovskaya puts it briefly: such partners do not hear each other. The World at the entry asks not for scale but for a check: do both of them live in this world, or is one of them only playing at being there?

The same wish has a reverse side. A world built to one person's design turns into a workshop where the other is remade to fit the plan: the right friends, the right interests, the right faith. Whatever does not fit the design is quietly cut away, and the whole world for two becomes very small.
In Waite's list of divinatory meanings, the World includes "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place". In the myth, the flight on that list happens literally.

sections.h2: The Sun in the middle: a light that makes eyes close
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple travels from the shared wish to the main task: what it does and what it goes through. This is how the site reads it; for Lisovskaya it is an "addition" to the main task. Here stands the Sun, and this couple's road is bright.

The Sun in a couple means warmth, success, a house that always has guests, children, shared victories and the feeling that someone reliable is close by. Waite's divinatory list for the Sun has three entries: "Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment." Benebell Wen is even more direct: "a radiant marriage, perhaps one to a spouse with a successful career", "a power couple". The middle of the tail holds the card of a happy marriage, and the myth tells what such a marriage costs.

"Sañjñā used to shut her eyes when the Sun gazed on her": so the story begins in the Markandeya Purana, in F. E. Pargiter's translation (1904). The Sun answers in anger: because you always close your eyes when you see me, you will give birth to Yama, "the imprisoner of mankind". The Sun is no villain. He shines as he can and wants to be looked at: for Wen, the Sun is a card "about dominance and captivating the attention and respect of others". But the one beside him cannot look into direct light. "It was with pain that Sañjñā, the noble lady, endured the Sun's splendour," the text says, and then come her questions: "What am I to do? Where am I to go? Where shall I go that I may find ease? And how shall the Sun, my husband, control his wrath?"

The scene is a familiar one. One partner is the sun: work, projects, friends, energy, and the house revolves around them. The other basks in it at first, then grows tired of being lit up all the time and starts to squint: falls silent, agrees, withdraws. The first sees only the closed eyelids and feels hurt: "You won't even look at me." Of everything Lisovskaya writes about the Sun among a couple's tasks, one thing matters most here: not knowing how to talk about problems. Sañjñā does not say a single word to her husband. She goes straight to making a shadow.

The instructions she leaves the shadow are frightening in their precision: "Remain thou here in the Sun's house even as I; and behave thou becomingly to the children even as to the Sun. And though questioned say nothing of this my going away; say always this, 'I am she indeed, Sañjñā by name.'" And the shadow agrees to keep the secret "as far as suffering my hair to be seized and as far as undergoing curses".

In a living couple the shadow is the partner who goes on doing everything properly — dinners, school runs, a smile for the guests, "everything's fine" — while they themselves have long been elsewhere. The shadow is obedient, friendly and recognisable at first sight; she is "of the same colour". In the myth the Sun lives with her for a long time, three children are born, and all the while the Sun takes Chhāyā for his wife Sañjñā, as the Vishnu Purana says. The substitution is given away by a small thing nobody planned: the shadow is fonder of her own children than of the others. Yama, offended, raises his foot at her, she curses him, and the boy runs to his father: "this great marvel was never seen by any one, that a mother casting love away imprecates a curse on her son."

In the myth the Sun is the husband and the wife is the one who leaves a shadow. In a living couple this is not divided by sex and not fixed forever: either partner can shine, either can slip into the shadow, sometimes by turns. The tail belongs to the couple, not to the one who shines.

What the numbers are made of explains where this Sun gets its force. In the main variant it is built from The Tower and The Empress, a sudden blow and abundance. The same light that makes a home and children grow can also blind.

sections.h2: The Chariot as the main task: two horses instead of a sun and a shadow
paragraphs: A couple's main task is read mostly through its minus, through what does not work and what has to be learned. With the Chariot in a couple the minus is easy to recognise: anger that immediately looks for someone to punish, and running alone instead of a shared road. The myth has both, and it shows where they lead.

Anger settles nothing. The Sun curses his wife for closing her eyes, the shadow curses the son, and the Sun is ready to curse the shadow too. Reversed, Waite's Chariot means "Riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat", and that is what a house looks like when everyone answers with force. Not one curse brings Sañjñā back.

Something else does. The Sun learns where she is: among the Northern Kurus, in the shape of a mare, practising austerities. And he understands why she went there. The Markandeya Purana records the purpose of her austerities in a single line: "May my husband become mild in body, beautiful in form." She ran not away from him but so that it would be possible to live beside him. And the Sun does what she never once asked for aloud: "Pare down my splendour now," he tells his father-in-law.

Then the Sun takes the form of a horse and goes north. Sañjñā, not recognising him and afraid of a stranger, "went towards him face to face, intent on guarding her rear". They meet nose to nose, the way horses meet, and from that meeting the Ashvins are born. Only then does the Sun show his true form, "and she gazing upon his true form felt a keen joy". Both return home in their own shapes.

This is the whole of this couple's Chariot. The one who shines turns down the light himself, by his own will and in measure. The one who ran stops running and turns to face the other, but still guards her back: a face-to-face conversation does not require surrendering one's boundaries. They meet not as a sun and a shadow but as two horses, as equals. And each keeps their own run. Sañjñā's austerities among the Northern Kurus are not a betrayal of the marriage but her own path. This is exactly the plus of the Chariot in a couple: each has their own work and their own growth outside the home, clear roles and decisions made together.

The Chariot itself was once read as the sun. Waite reports that Court de Gébelin saw in it "Osiris Triumphing, the conquering sun in spring-time having vanquished the obstacles of winter", and he does not agree. In the 21-19-7 tail the Chariot comes after the Sun, and its meaning is the opposite: it is the place where the Sun stops conquering. He crosses the sky every day. A home cannot be conquered that way.

Lisovskaya writes that a couple with the Chariot looks, from outside, more like friends and a team than like lovers. The Indian wedding rite ends with the same word. Bride and groom take seven steps together, and after the seventh come the words "Friend! be with seven steps (united to me)" (Paraskara Grihya Sutra, I, 8, 1, in Hermann Oldenberg's translation). Seven is the number of the Chariot. This is a coincidence, not proof, but its sense is exact: this couple's main task is to become companions who walk in step.

sections.h2: The Ashvins: a wagon made of mind and wheels made of hearing
paragraphs: The children of that meeting are the Ashvins, "the Horsemen", twin riders. In the Rigveda they have a three-wheeled chariot, and in it they come to the most famous wedding of the Vedic hymns, the wedding of Surya, the Sun's daughter (X, 85). Verses of this hymn are still recited at Indian weddings, and the bride's wagon is described in it like this (our literal translation):
"Her mind was the wagon, heaven was its cover… Thy two ears were the wheels… breath was fitted in as the axle. Surya mounted the wagon made of mind as she set out for her husband."

This is an answer to the myth about her family. In Saranyu's story nobody hears anybody: she keeps silent, he does not notice, the shadow repeats her learned line, "I am she indeed". In the hymn the wheels of the wedding wagon are made of hearing. This couple's Chariot runs on the same thing: the ability to listen.

Another stanza of the same hymn reads like a riddle: "The Brahmans, by their seasons, know, O Sūrya, those two wheels of thine: One kept concealed, those only who are skilled in highest truths have learned." Read as a parable about a couple, the two visible wheels are the two people. The third, hidden one is what lies between them, and it is what keeps the chariot moving. This is how a 21-19-7 couple learns to travel: not on one partner's light and the other's shadow, but on three wheels, one of which is never shown to anyone.

The hymn ends with a blessing that suits this couple better than any advice: "Be ye not parted; dwell ye here; reach the full time of human life." And in its last stanza: "So may the Universal Gods, so may the Waters join our hearts."

sections.h2: What Waite's cards show: two children under the sun and a sun on the angel's brow
paragraphs: Waite's Sun is a naked child on a white horse. But Waite himself writes that in older cards two children stood under the sun by a water, "gambolling, or running hand in hand", and that Éliphas Lévi said these are sometimes replaced by "a naked child mounted on a white horse". The Sun of the old deck is a card of two. In the same Rigveda wedding hymn the Sun and the Moon are called two playing children going round the sacrifice: "One of the Pair beholdeth all existing things; the other ordereth seasons and is born again" (X, 85, 18).
Reversed, the Sun in Waite's divinatory list means "The same in a lesser sense". The Sun of the myth, once cut down, looks just like that: it shines less but is still the Sun.

Temperance, the card of the centre in 97.8% of these couples, Waite opens with the words "A winged angel, with the sign of the sun upon his forehead". And he adds at once that "it is, moreover, untrue to say that the figure symbolizes the genius of the sun, though it is the analogy of solar light". Here the sun does not blind; it is a sign on the brow of the one who is "pouring the essences of life from chalice to chalice".

Waite's Chariot is drawn by two sphinxes, but "in the eighteenth century", he writes, "white horses were yoked to the car". And Benebell Wen notices on Waite's chariot an Indian emblem, the lingam and yoni, a union of two principles, and writes that it continues "certain themes that ran through Key 6: The Lovers". The Lovers are the values of most couples with this tail.

sections.h2: The couple's centre: Temperance, or the Sun on the lathe
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the shared atmosphere between the partners, what is inside and not for show. In 97.8% of couples with the 21-19-7 tail it is Temperance, in 2.2% The Hierophant.

Temperance is the myth's answer to the question of what to do with a Sun that is too bright. In the Vishnu Purana, Vishvakarman puts the Sun on his lathe and grinds off part of his radiance: "and in this manner reduced it an eighth, for more than that was inseparable" (H. H. Wilson's translation, 1840). In the Markandeya Purana the craftsman pares away fifteen parts out of sixteen, and the Sun keeps one. The Puranas disagree about the measure. They agree on the main thing: the light is reduced, not put out. The Sun cannot stop being himself entirely. In the Matsya Purana, as Wilson notes, the craftsman trimmed the sun "every where except in the feet, the extent of which he could not discern".

The light that was cut away was not lost. From it Vishvakarman forged the discus of Vishnu, the trident of Shiva and the weapons of other gods, all "from the superfluous rays of the sun". This is our reading, but for a couple it is exact: one partner's surplus of brightness does not have to blind, nor does it have to vanish. It can be given over to protecting both.

Lisovskaya describes the atmosphere of Temperance as arguments settled by talking and an understanding of what the other needs. For Wen, Temperance comes to "cool what was too hot, heat up what was too cold", and in a relationship it calls for "a greater need for cooperation and tempering of extreme emotions, such as anger, resentment, hostility". Lisovskaya describes the minus of Temperance in a couple in a single phrase, and it sounds like a retelling of the myth: one partner always gives way, and the other does not even notice. That is the house of the Sun and the Shadow.

In rare couples the centre holds The Hierophant: tradition, order, doing things "properly". In the myth it has a voice too, Sañjñā's father: "Dwelling a long time among kinsmen brings no good repute to women; kinsmen hold a woman's proper residence is in her husband's house." Advice by the rules solved nothing: the daughter went not home but north.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: A couple's values are its shared path and what the two are together for. In 60.3% of couples with this tail the values are The Lovers, in 39.7% The Devil.

For Wen, The Lovers is first of all a choice, not romance: "in every traditional interpretation of The Lovers, the card is about a moral choice". The myth has two choices, and both are turning points: the Sun chooses to reduce his light, Sañjñā chooses to turn and face him. The myth begins with closed eyes and ends with a gaze: "she gazing upon his true form felt a keen joy". For this couple the value of The Lovers is to look at each other openly, without squinting and without pretending.

The Devil in the values speaks of something else: a role that holds like a chain. The shadow agreed to play someone else's life until her hair was seized. Lisovskaya's closing thought on The Devil in a couple is that "nobody belongs to anybody", and in its plus this card accepts the dark sides and forgives mistakes. That is exactly what the myth does with the shadow: she is not driven out. Her children receive their places: one son becomes the planet Shani, another will be one of the future Manus, and her daughter becomes the river Tapati. A shadow that has a place of her own no longer needs to pass herself off as someone else.

sections.h2: How to live the 21-19-7 tail: what changes the story
paragraphs: The myth does not promise the couple a happy ending. It shows the places where the story turns.

ul: **Speak about the light out loud.** Sañjñā never once tells her husband that it is hard for her; she goes straight to making a shadow. Saying "it blinds me" is harder than withdrawing, but only that gives the other a chance to turn the light down.

**Notice the shadow.** If one partner has long been answering "everything's fine" and doing everything properly while not really being there, this is not peace in the couple but a copy of it "of the same colour".
**Turn down the light by choice and in measure.** The Sun asks to be pared down himself, and an eighth is ground away: "more than that was inseparable". There is no need to put oneself out entirely.
**Do not bring anyone back with anger.** Not one curse in the myth mended anything. A visit to the craftsman and the shape of a horse did.
**Meet face to face while guarding one's back.** A hard conversation does not require surrendering one's boundaries.
**Leave each partner their own run.** Each needs time and work where the other's light does not reach. Sañjñā's Northern Kurus are not a betrayal of the union but her own path.
**Travel in the wagon made of mind.** Its wheels are ears.

paragraphs: If there are threats in the couple, if one partner fears for their safety or there is violence, this is no longer a matter of the tail. It calls for professional help, and in danger, a call to a local emergency number.

ul: **21 · The World — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: a whole world of its own — a home, the road, a shared view of life in which everything fits. This is the couple's common language and its first resistance: in a whole world it is easy to miss that one of the two no longer lives there.

**19 · The Sun — middle of the task.** How the couple moves towards its goal: warmly, brightly, with success, guests and children, to the envy of others. The risk is one partner's light, which makes the other start closing their eyes.

**7 · The Chariot — main task.** What the couple has to learn: to travel together instead of taking turns to shine and to run. The card's minus is anger and running alone; its plus is two people who run side by side, each at their own pace, and steer together.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 21-19-7 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a task for the couple, not for one person. The couple enters it wanting a whole world for two (The World), travels the road brightly, warmly and in full view (The Sun), and has to learn the Chariot: to travel together as equals, so that one partner's brightness does not drive the other into the shadow and running away does not replace talking.

faq.q: Can the 21-19-7 tail appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the reduced sum of the entry and the main task, so with an entry of 21 and a task of 7 it would be 10, The Wheel of Fortune. The Sun in the middle comes only from adding the middles of two people.

faq.q: Which partner is the Sun, and which one slips into the shadow?
faq.a: The tail does not say: it is one tail for two. Either partner can shine, either can slip into the shadow, and the roles change over time. Sex has nothing to do with it, even though in the myth the Sun is the husband.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a relationship?
faq.a: The tail does not predict a couple's fate and does not pass judgement on it. It shows the task the two of them work on together. In the myth the story ends with a return home, after the Sun has reduced his light and his wife has turned to face him.

faq.q: Are there other couple tails made of the same numbers?
faq.a: No. The entry of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 7 and 19 cannot come first, and the order 21-7-19 does not occur for any pair of dates. 21-19-7 is the only tail made of these three cards.

faq.q: Where does the story of the Sun's wife come from?
faq.a: From the Rigveda (X, 17, 1–2), where it fits into two stanzas, and from the Puranas, where it is told in full: the Markandeya Purana (cantos 77–78) and the Vishnu Purana (III, 2). The wedding hymn of Surya is Rigveda X, 85. The Rigveda is quoted in Ralph Griffith's translation except for the wagon stanzas, which are our own literal translation; the Markandeya Purana in F. E. Pargiter's, the Vishnu Purana in H. H. Wilson's.

report.h3: The whole world at the wedding, and a substitution nobody noticed

report: At the entry to this couple's task stands the World. It is the couple's common language and shared wish, and the wish is the size of the world: a home, the road, other countries, a shared view of life in which everything fits. From outside, such couples often look perfect.

The Rigveda adds a detail that is unsettling. The bride vanished in the wedding procession itself, "as she was carried to her dwelling", and nobody noticed, because she was replaced by "one like her". The shared plans and shared friends are still there, but one partner has long been the only one talking about "our world", while the other nods.

The bride is Saranyu, "the Swift One", and in later texts Sañjñā, a word whose meanings include "agreement, mutual understanding". The double is called Chhāyā, "Shadow". What stands at the couple's entry is agreement, and agreement is the first thing to leave.

report.h3: A light that makes the eyes close

report.h3: The Sun who asked to be pared down

report: The main task is the Chariot, and it is read through what does not work. Anger settles nothing here: the Sun curses his wife for closing her eyes, the shadow curses the son, and not one curse brings Sañjñā back.

And each keeps their own run: time and work where the other's light does not reach.

report.h3: A wagon whose wheels are ears

report: The children of that meeting are the Ashvins, twin horsemen with a three-wheeled chariot. They come to the wedding of Surya, the Sun's daughter, and in that Rigveda hymn the bride's wagon is described like this: "Her mind was the wagon… Thy two ears were the wheels… breath was fitted in as the axle." In Sañjñā's story nobody heard anybody: she kept silent, he did not notice, the shadow repeated her learned line. In the hymn the wheels are made of hearing.

The same hymn says that the Brahmans know two of the wheels, while the third is concealed and known only to those skilled in the highest truths. Read as a parable about a couple, the two wheels are the two people, and the third is what lies between them. That is what keeps the chariot moving.

For a couple with this tail the myth yields a few rules: speak about the light out loud instead of closing one's eyes; notice when "everything's fine" has become a shadow; turn down one's own brightness without putting oneself out entirely; bring no one back with anger; leave each partner their own run. If there are threats in the couple, if one partner fears for their safety or there is violence, this is no longer a matter of the tail: it calls for professional help, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

unit.title: Two horses, not sun and shadow

captions.M: Want a whole world for two where everything fits
captions.N: Shine brightly without driving the other into shadow
captions.D: Travel as equals: turn down the light, don't run

unit.meaning: Your task is to travel as equals: turn down your own light and speak up instead of slipping into the shadow.
